spatial_claims.claim: BC is a straight line; D divides BC into segments BD and DC
E is the midpoint of BC (bisects BC), so BE = EC
D is a different division point from E, so BC is cut into unequal segments at D
By II.5, BD·DC + ED² = BE² (rectangle on unequal segments plus square on segment between cuts equals square on half)
FG is a separate straight line equal to twice DE
BD = BE + ED and DC = BE - ED, placing D between E and C on segment BC (order B, E, D, C)

configuration_map: All points lie on a single line segment BC. E is the midpoint of BC. D lies between E and C, so the collinear order is B, E, D, C. FG is a separate line segment defined as 2·DE. The entire configuration is one-dimensional with no angles, triangles, circles, or interior/exterior relationships. All algebraic identities (II.5, commensurability propositions) are applied to segments on this line.
pass_reason: The proof is fundamentally algebraic, dealing with commensurability of line segments. The only spatial configuration is collinear points on segment BC (order B, E, D, C) and a separate segment FG. All spatial claims are trivially consistent: E as midpoint, D between E and C, and the II.5 identity all cohere. There are no angle decompositions, no triangle interior/exterior arguments, no circle configurations -- nothing that could harbor a spatial contradiction.
